chapter: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York
title: Mr. Bellson's tears: the police tell him to remove his Black house guests
summary: Louis Bellson's father, ashamed, tells Simmons the police ordered the guests out.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yes. That's what we were club-hopping. We were looking for a piano player, a musician. We couldn't find one. So we had to go back to Rock Island without one. So we waited until, well, not the first train, but the last train that was running that would put us there on time to go to work. You know, just go straight to work. But instead of me getting off in Rock Island I got off in Moline, Louis' home. I said to Charlie, I said, "They might have a bandwagon there to meet us, you know, when we get off the train." He said, "Oh, no, man," like that. He said, "I'm going on, from the train station to the job." I said, "Okay, I'll see you there." So I went
MS. WILLARD: Mr. Bellson being Louis Bellson's father.

Yes. And when I got there he was crying crocodile tears. I mean, actually tears. He said, "The police has been here," and he says, "How do you say this word?" He couldn't even say it. I knew the word he meant, you know. He said, what are you doing with them here in your home? He said, "We have house guests." He said, "Well, you don't have any nigger house guests. Get them out of your house." Now, he said, "If this was my neighbors on either side of me," he said, "I'd kill them with my bare hands," he says, "but I've had my music store here for about 25 years, I've raised my family here and my roots are here, and I can't fight the police. You boys will have to go." He says, "I'm very sorry. Nothing like this has ever happened to me in my life." And he's still crying. He's sobbing. His shoulders is going up and down while he's talking, you know. So I got on the phone. Charlie's had time to get to the club. I told Charlie, I says, "Come and get your things." He laughed, "What do you mean, man?" I said, "Come and get your things." He said, "Well, you've got to tell me more than that." I said, "I don't have to tell you any more of anything. Come and get your clothes." He said, "All right, man. I'll be there in a few minutes." In a few minutes he was there, because you could go through all

three of these cities in 15 minutes. All he had to do was get a cab and he'd be there in five minutes. But I walked. Afterward, from Rock Island to Moline, with my bass and my wet clothes and everything else, getting out of town, trying to get out of town. But I got away from that club.
